HRUI Showcases Industrial Networking at CDIIF 2026
2026-03-13
Chengdu, China – March 11-13, 2026 – HRUI showcased multiple series of networking communication devices and industry solutions at the Chengdu International Industry Fair (CDIIF), demonstrating its technical expertise in network equipment R&D, manufacturing, and customized OEM/ODM services.
The exhibition brought together leading manufacturers and technology innovators to explore new opportunities in intelligent manufacturing and industrial transformation.
During the event, HRUI presented a range of networking products, including industrial (Bypass) switches, 100G/10G high-speed switches, and managed switches for industrial and commercial networks. These solutions support applications in industrial control, intelligent transportation, energy and power systems, data centers, and enterprise networks.
In industrial automation environments, HRUI networking solutions provide reliable connectivity for smart motors, CNC machines, variable-frequency drives, industrial robots, PLC systems, and other industrial equipment, ensuring stable communication across production systems.
HRUI also highlighted its one-stop OEM/ODM capabilities, offering end-to-end support from product definition and hardware design to software customization, mechanical design, and mass production.
Through continued innovation in industrial networking technologies, HRUI remains committed to advancing industrial digitalization and intelligent manufacturing.

HRUI Showcases Industrial Communication Solutions at CEIC 2026
2026-03-27
Fuzhou, China – March 26–27, 2026 – HRUI showcased its industrial communication portfolio and tailored solutions for highway digital infrastructure at the China Expressway Informatization Conference and Technology & Product Exhibition (CEIC 2026), highlighting capabilities in device connectivity and intelligent monitoring under the theme “New Stage, New Technology, New Pattern.
Designed for harsh outdoor highway environments, HRUI solutions operate across a wide temperature range (-40°C to +75°C) and feature IP40 protection, PoE watchdog, and rapid ring network self-healing (<50 ms). These capabilities ensure reliable communications in applications such as tunnel monitoring, ETC gantries, smart toll stations, and vehicle-to-infrastructure deployments, underscoring HRUI’s expertise in industrial networking.
Throughout the event, the HRUI team met with industry professionals for technical exchanges and solution discussions. Visitors expressed interest in technologies including PTP 1588 precise time synchronization and TSN (Time-Sensitive Networking). Product reliability, together with the team’s technical support, received positive feedback from attendees.
Participation in CEIC 2026 highlighted HRUI’s engineering capabilities and industry experience. The company will continue to advance communication solutions for smart transportation, supporting the ongoing digital transformation of highway infrastructure.

Understanding Core Switch: What It Is and How to Choose the Right One for Your Network.
In the realm of system networking, three key types of switches are frequently mentioned: access switches, aggregation switches, and core switches. The part of the network that directly connects to user devices is referred to as the access layer. The layer that lies between the access layer and the core layer is known as the distribution or aggregation layer, while the backbone of the network is termed the core layer.

h1: HRUI 6 Ports Gigabit Managed Industrial PoE Switch
pages.description: HRUI 6-port Gigabit Industrial Ethernet PoE Switch, HR600-BTGM-42AS, is designed for exceptional performance in the toughest environments. This robust switch features four Gigabit BT PoE ports, delivering a maximum power output of 90W, and two 2.5G SFP ports compatible with 1.25G/155M.
headings: HRUI 6 Ports Gigabit Managed Industrial PoE Switch
tables: Offer 4 PoE ports with a maximum output power of 90W per port, enabling simultaneous transmission of both power and data signals to end devices over a single Cat.5e or higher Ethernet cable, eliminating the need for separate power cables and simplifying installation and maintenance.

This Gigabit Industrial Switch features two 2.5G Base-X SFP ports and offers an increased switching capacity for non-blocking high-speed data forwarding. It supports high-bandwidth connections and is compatible with auto-adaptive fiber optic modules for 155M, 1G, 1.25G, and 2.5G, providing a broader range of data rates.

The device features IP40 protection and a rugged high-strength metal case, designed for reliable operation in demanding industrial environments. It supports DIN35 rail mounting and boasts an EMC grade 4 design, ensuring resilience against electromagnetic interference. With a working temperature range of -40℃ to 75℃, it is built to withstand harsh conditions while delivering optimal performance.

The device features dual power input, enabling you to set up multiple power sources for enhanced reliability and redundancy. This design guarantees that your system stays operational during power failures or unexpected shutdowns.
Support port management, ACL, QoS, VLANS, RSTP, STP, VLAN, LACP, LLDP, Multicast and more.

The HR600-BTGM-42AS is designed to support the ERPS ring and boasts a robust self-recovery capability that operates within 12ms. This feature helps prevent interruptions and external threats, significantly improving system reliability and uptime across diverse environments.
• Integrated PoE Features for Managing PD

Designed as a managed PoE switch for surveillance, wireless, and VoIP networks, the HR600-BTGM-42AS offers several advanced PoE management features, including: • PoE Watchdog • PoE Configuration • PoE Schedule • PoE Timer Management
Detect and reboot dropped or unresponsive PoE-powered devices.

Provide configuration support for PoE settings, including parameters such as temperature, type, level, power, current, total PoE power budget management, PoE power control, port priority allocations, and individualized power limits for each PoE port. This thorough strategy will optimize PoE management, promote efficient resource utilization, and improve device reliability and performance.

Support for customizing the schedule to turn the PoE function on or off based on specific needs. This flexibility not only helps optimize energy consumption but also reduces operational costs, making it an efficient solution for energy management.

Support rebooting the PoE function of port during a specified time. This will help reduce device crashes caused by buffer overflow, ensuring more reliable and stable performance during designated time intervals.

The HR600-BTGM-42AS supports both IPv6 and IPv4 protocols, enabling SMBs to transition to the IPv6 era with minimal investment. There's no need to replace or overhaul existing network infrastructure when implementing the IPv6 networking.

The HR600-BTGM-42AS features advanced cybersecurity measures, including SSHv2 and SNMPv3 protocols, to protect against cyber threats. Its robust security capabilities enhance switch management while maintaining cost-effective deployment for critical network operations.

Support for Fiber Module DDM (Digital Diagnostic Monitoring) includes tracking key parameters such as transceiver supply voltage, temperature, transmitter bias current, transmitter output power, and received optical power. By analyzing these metrics, you can effectively diagnose issues that may be affecting the transceiver optics' performance.
The HR600-BTGM-42AS is perfectly suited for telecommunications and Carrier Ethernet applications, compatible with IEEE 1588 and synchronous Ethernet.

Understanding Core Switch: What It Is and How to Choose the Right One for Your Network.
2025-04-03
In the realm of system networking, three key types of switches are frequently mentioned: access switches, aggregation switches, and core switches. The part of the network that directly connects to user devices is referred to as the access layer. The layer that lies between the access layer and the core layer is known as the distribution or aggregation layer, while the backbone of the network is termed the core layer. This article delves into the concept of core switches and offers guidance on selecting the right one for your network.
What is a Core Switch?
A core switch is not merely a type of switch but rather denotes the switch that operates at the core layer (the network's backbone). Positioned at the top of the three-layer network architecture, it functions like a senior management team in an organization, tasked primarily with efficiently routing data from the aggregation layer. Core switches are critical for establishing a fast and reliable network architecture through high-speed data forwarding.
Typically, core switches are Layer 3 switches equipped with robust network management capabilities. They are characterized by numerous ports and high bandwidth, offering greater reliability, redundancy, throughput, and lower latency compared to access and aggregation switches. For a network with over 100 computers, a core switch is indispensable for ensuring stability and high performance.
Factors to Consider When Choosing a Core Switch
When selecting a core switch, it’s essential to focus on several crucial aspects that can significantly impact the performance and reliability of your network. Here are key factors to consider:
Port Type, Rate, and Quantity
Evaluate the required port types, speeds, and quantities based on your existing aggregation layer switch. If budget permits, opt for a core switch with diverse port types and a higher number of ports. For instance, a switch equipped with 10 Gigabit uplink ports or stacking ports can accommodate future network expansion.
Backplane Bandwidth
For core switches, if you want to achieve full-duplex non-blocking, you must meet the minimum standard requirements (backplane bandwidth = port number * port rate * 2), the higher the backplane bandwidth, the faster the data exchange, the core switch The stronger the data processing capability.
Forwarding Rate
The core switch plays a pivotal role in managing substantial network traffic, necessitating a forwarding rate that typically outpaces that of access and aggregation switches. To calculate the required forwarding rate for a core switch, you can use the following formula:
**Forwarding Rate = Mpps + (Number of Gigabit Ports × 1.488 Mpps) + (Number of 100-Megabit Ports × 0.1488 Mpps)**.
It's essential to consider that the forwarding rate needed by a core switch is directly influenced by the number of devices connected to the network. Rather than making arbitrary selections, it's advisable to analyze various traffic reports and assess user group patterns. This careful consideration helps prevent potential network bottlenecks and avoids unnecessary resource expenditure.
For Layer 3 switches, a switch is deemed qualified when both the backplane bandwidth and the forwarding rate meet or exceed the minimum standard requirements. This ensures optimal performance and reliability in handling network traffic.
Link Aggregation
Link aggregation combines multiple physical ports into a single logical port, enhancing bandwidth and maintaining network stability. It's advisable to choose a core switch with link aggregation capabilities to ensure efficient transmission of traffic from the aggregation switch to the core switch.
VLAN and QoS Support
As global data traffic grows, the demand for voice, video, and data traffic increases, leading to potential issues such as network congestion. Relying solely on increased bandwidth is not a sustainable solution. VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) allow for effective segmentation of different applications, while QoS (Quality of Service) prioritizes real-time and critical traffic, helping to alleviate delay and congestion issues. Thus, selecting a core switch that supports VLANs and QoS is both economical and efficient.
Redundant Performance
Redundancy in a core switch is vital for safeguarding network security. It's essential to choose a switch that offers substantial redundancy to ensure a seamless switch-over in case of hardware failure, thereby preventing network outages. Key redundancy features to look for include port, module, and power supply redundancy, as well as routing redundancy through protocols like HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) and VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol), which provide backup solutions and enhance network stability.
Security Features
Given that the core layer serves as the network’s backbone, it is critical to choose a core switch with robust security features. Effective security measures may include network management functions like ACLs (Access Control Lists) and flow control, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) protection to mitigate spoofing attacks, and VPN (Virtual Private Network) capabilities to secure communications between corporate intranets.
Additional Parameters to Consider
Beyond the aforementioned factors, consider other functionalities such as stacking and hot backup. These features are significant in determining the performance, efficiency, and stability of core switches in real-world applications. A core switch is pivotal in maintaining the integrity of the entire network; a catastrophic failure could lead to extensive downtime and losses.

Exploring Which Wires in 100Mbps and 1000Mbps Network Cables Are Using to Transit Power In a PoE System
2024-12-25
Introduction
Power over Ethernet (PoE) technology has revolutionized the way we deploy network devices by allowing both data and power to be delivered over the same Ethernet cable. This innovation has not only simplified installation processes but also opened avenues for powering devices like IP cameras, VoIP phones, and wireless access points. To fully understand how PoE operates, it is essential to explore the network cables involved, particularly how different wires in 100Mbps (Fast Ethernet) and 1000Mbps (Gigabit Ethernet) cables contribute to PoE functionality.
Ethernet Cable Standards
Before diving into the specifics of wire utilization in PoE systems, it is important to familiarize ourselves with Ethernet cable categories:
Cat 5e:
Supports 100Mbps and is typically used for Fast Ethernet. It can also support 1000Mbps (Gigabit Ethernet) for short distances.
Cat 6:
Better performance over longer distances, supports 1000Mbps (Gigabit Ethernet) up to 100 meters with improved crosstalk performance.
Cat 6a and Cat 7:
Designed for higher frequencies, providing better shielding and supporting higher speeds and PoE applications.
Wire Configuration
Category 5e and 6 cables typically use four twisted pairs of wires. Each pair consists of two wires:
Pair 1: White/Blue and Blue
Pair 2: White/Orange and Orange
Pair 3: White/Green and Green
Pair 4: White/Brown and Brown
PoE Standards
The IEEE has defined several standards for Power over Ethernet:
IEEE 802.3af:
Delivers up to 15.4 Watts of power (12.95 Watts guaranteed at the powered device) and requires at least 2 pairs of wires.
IEEE 802.3at (PoE+):
Increases power delivery capability to 30 Watts (25.5 Watts guaranteed), also using at least 2 pairs of wires.
IEEE 802.3bt (PoE++):
Introduces higher power levels, supporting up to 60 Watts (Type 3) and 100 Watts (Type 4). This standard can utilize all 4 pairs of wires.
Wires Utilization in Different Ethernet Cables
100Mbps (Cat 5/5e)
In traditional 100Mbps networks, PoE devices primarily utilize the first two pairs of wires, designated as:
Pair 1 (Pins 1 and 2): Transmits data.
Pair 2 (Pins 3 and 6): Transmits data and carries power under IEEE 802.3af and 802.3at standards.
The other pairs (Pair 3 and Pair 4) are not typically used for data transmission in 100Mbps connections. Instead, they can be reserved for auxiliary functions or, in certain PoE applications, can carry additional power (if the infrastructure supports it).
PoE Standards
The IEEE has defined several standards for Power over Ethernet:
IEEE 802.3af:
Delivers up to 15.4 Watts of power (12.95 Watts guaranteed at the powered device) and requires at least 2 pairs of wires.
IEEE 802.3at (PoE+):
Increases power delivery capability to 30 Watts (25.5 Watts guaranteed), also using at least 2 pairs of wires.
IEEE 802.3bt (PoE++):
Introduces higher power levels, supporting up to 60 Watts (Type 3) and 100 Watts (Type 4). This standard can utilize all 4 pairs of wires.
1000Mbps (Gigabit Ethernet, Cat 5e and above)
At 1000Mbps, also known as Gigabit Ethernet, PoE implementations change slightly. All four pairs of wires are used for data transmission.
Pair 1 (Pins 1 and 2): Transmits data.
In terms of PoE power delivery, all 4 pairs can be utilized, especially for higher power standards (IEEE 802.3at and IEEE 802.3bt):
For IEEE 802.3af, power delivery typically uses Pair 1 and Pair 2.
For IEEE 802.3at, power can still use just these two pairs or all four pairs for optimal efficiency.
For IEEE 802.3bt, all four pairs (with Type 3 and Type 4) can distribute power simultaneously, allowing for a more powerful PoE solution.

Discover The Advantages Of Industrial Switch
2024-12-26
Industrial switches offer enhanced functionalities compared to standard commercial switches, featuring a more diverse and flexible port configuration and product lineup that cater to the varied needs of different industrial sectors. They are commonly utilized in areas such as smart transportation, security surveillance, renewable energy like wind and solar, as well as in mining operations. Notably, power generation, transportation, and metallurgy are identified as key industries with significant potential for industrial switch applications. Let's delve into the primary advantages of industrial switches and guidelines for selecting the right one.
Advantages of Industrial Switches
Exceptional Anti-Interference Capabilities
Industrial switches are designed with robust anti-interference features, including high levels of protection against lightning, water, corrosion, and static electricity—capabilities not typically found in commercial switches.
Use of Industrial-Grade Components
Constructed to endure challenging environments, industrial switches utilize high-quality components, enabling them to excel in demanding industrial settings.
Wide Temperature Range
With metal casings for improved heat dissipation and enhanced protection, industrial switches can function reliably within a temperature spectrum of -45 to +75°C. This adaptability to extreme temperature and humidity contrasts with the tighter operational limits of commercial switches.
Fast Ring Network Redundancy
Industrial switches support fast ring network configurations with a redundancy recovery time of less than 20 milliseconds. In comparison, commercial switches typically have much longer recovery times ranging from 10 to 30 seconds, making them unsuitable for fast-paced industrial applications.
Dual Power Supply Design
To mitigate the risks associated with power outages, industrial switches are equipped with redundant power supply systems that ensure stable and reliable performance. Conversely, commercial switches usually rely on a single AC power source, which may not suffice in industrial contexts.
Extended Service Life
Crafted with industrial-grade materials and engineering, these switches boast higher reliability and longer lifespans, generally exceeding 10 years, while standard commercial switches typically last between 3 to 5 years.
Key Factors for Selecting an Industrial Switch
Reliability
Reliability is paramount in industrial environments. Essential factors include the hardware's ability to withstand working conditions such as temperature ranges, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), lightning protection ratings, installation requirements, power supply options, fanless designs, redundancy, and fault recovery capabilities. Detailed specifications on operating temperature, electromagnetic protection, and lightning ratings should be available in product documentation.
Real-Time Performance
Data transmission in network applications can incur delays. When selecting an industrial Ethernet switch, it's crucial to consider the port delay associated with data frame forwarding. In standard factory automation scenarios, a response time of less than 20 milliseconds is preferable. Thus, the switch port delay should ideally be under 20 microseconds.
Compatibility
Industrial Ethernet switches must ensure compatibility with other industrial Ethernet devices using standard TCP/IP protocols. It’s essential that there are no discrepancies between industrial Ethernet and commercial Ethernet equipment. Furthermore, industrial Ethernet devices should be equipped to support various field bus solutions relevant to different industrial applications.
By understanding these advantages and selection criteria, you can make an informed decision when choosing industrial switches that best suit your operational needs.

ERPS Ring Network Protection Protocol
2024-12-26
1. What is ring network redundancy?
Ethernet ring network redundancy means that when the network cable connection is interrupted or the communication link fails, the switch can quickly activate its backup port after receiving the fault information, enable another sound communication link, and restore network communication. Normal operation greatly improves the continuity, stability and reliability of network communication.
2. Ethernet ring network category
At present, the common Ethernet ring network redundancy is mainly divided into the following types: ring network based on spanning tree STP/RSTP/MSTP protocol, ring network based on private ring network protocol, ring network based on ERPS (G.8032) general ring network protocol Ring.
At present, in the Ethernet of the Layer 2 network, the requirements for fault self-healing time are getting higher and higher. The STP/RSTP/MSTP spanning tree protocol cannot meet the convergence performance requirements of the link, and the manufacturer's private ring network protocol has a single networking form, and cannot be compatible with other manufacturers' equipment. The ERPS protocol absorbs the advantages of ring network protection technologies such as STP, optimizes the detection mechanism, and has fast convergence speed. At the same time, it has good compatibility and is the mainstream choice for switch equipment manufacturers in the market.
HRUI commercial managed switches, industrial managed switches and other products support the ring network redundancy technology based on the ERPS protocol, which greatly improves the flexibility of networking, and the failure convergence time is ≤12ms, ensuring high stability of front-end video data transmission sex.
3. ERPS ring network protocol
ERPS (Ethernet Ring Protection Switching, Ethernet Ring Protection Switching Protocol), also known as G.8032, is a protocol developed by ITU specifically for link-layer Ethernet ring protection. It is used for link backup and improving network performance. reliability. It can prevent the broadcast storm caused by the data loop when the Ethernet ring network is complete, and can quickly restore the communication between each node on the ring network when a link on the Ethernet ring is disconnected.
4. ERPS function application
4.1. Common networking topologies
Multiple switches form a ring network, and one of them is set as the RPL Owner node. When the link is normal, the RPL port is automatically blocked.
4.2. Link failure recovery
When it is detected that the ring network link is disconnected, the Owner node releases the RPL port, and realizes the link data switching within 12ms, and the video and data are not stuck.

The Key Differences Between Managed vs Unmanaged Switches
2024-12-26
Network switches are like the “brain” of a network. Therefore, choosing suitable and well-performing network switches is an important task for network managers. For a long time, many users feel confused that how to choose between a managed switch and unmanaged switch. Now the problem that users care much about—what is the Differences Between Managed Switches vs Unmanaged Switches—will be explored.
What Is Managed Switch or Unmanaged Switch?
■ Managed Switch
Managed switches are usually to deliver the most comprehensive functions for a network. Due to their diverse and rich features such as VLAN, CLI, SNMP, IP Routing, QoS, etc., managed switches are often used in the core layer in a network, especially in large and complex data centers. However, in order to meet different size of networks demands, there are some lightly managed switches in the market, which is also known as smart switches. These switches only have part capabilities of managed switches. When users have limited costs and do not need all the features of fully managed switch, smart switch offers them an optimal alternative.
■ Unmanaged Switch
Compared with managed switches, unmanaged switches seem to be more “brainless”. They are a type of plug & play Ethernet network switch. What users need to do is to plug them in and wait them to work. Because unmanaged switches require no configuration at all. Therefore, when users need a few ports on their home or in a conference room, unmanaged switch can be used as a simple desktop switch to satisfy their demand.
Key Differences Between Managed vs Unmanaged Switches
There are various types of managed and unmanaged switches in the market like HRUI managed / unmanaged switches etc. And opinions about applications of these network switches vary from person to person. What’s the difference between managed switches and unmanaged switches?As the name suggests, one of the key differences between a managed and unmanaged switch lies in its approach. A managed network switch provides flexibility to the network administrator to control, manage, and prioritize the LAN traffic. However, an unmanaged switch works like a plug and play switch which allows devices on the LAN to communicate with each other, without user intervention. The following points will help you understand other key points between these two network switches:
■ Freedom of Configuration:
The managed switches allow users to manage, configure, as well as monitor the LAN. They allow users to create new LANs and segregate smaller devices and help users manage the traffic effectively. Managed network switches come with advanced features that allow users to recover data in the event of failure of the device or network. They also allow data recovery.
Unmanaged switches may be easy to use, but they come with a fixed configuration, which means you cannot make changes to the networks. This is why it is most commonly used for startup businesses having limited data exchange.
■ Performance Management:
Unmanaged network switches are the plug and play type switches. They have built-in QoS services, which ensure their easy setup and utility. However, the managed network switches allow you to manage the performance by prioritizing the channels. It utilizes protocols such as Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) to monitor the ethernet network the performance of all devices connected on the LAN. The managed switch also uses SNMP to analyze the current performance of devices on the network through an easy-to-understand graphical interface. Additionally, SNMP also enables remote management of the connected devices and network, without requiring a physical intervention on the switch.
■ Security Features:
Unmanaged switches have basic security features such as a lockable port cover that ensures basic security, and helps avoid any type of direct tampering on the device. However, managed network switches are equipped with advanced features that help identify active threats and shut them down on time, and protect data and control.
■ Costs:
The unmanaged network switches are available in affordable price ranges, whereas the managed switches are available in higher price ranges owing to their advanced features.

HRUI Industrial Redundant Ring Technology And Solution
2024-12-26
Industrial network failures pose a significant safety and economical risk. While no network is completely failproof, backup systems can help minimize these risks. As such, redundancy has become widely recognized as an essential aspect of any industrial network. There are many different ways to enhance redundancy in a network. One way is by relying on a redundant ring topology.
■ Ring topology
When relying on a redundant ring, an important factor to consider is how the topology of the ring relates to the network’s physical layout. Another factor to consider is the recovery time, the recovery time is much more critical in industrial applications than commercial ones.
First, let’s start with a general overview of ring topology.
A ring topology is a network configuration where each networked device is connected to two other devices on either side of it to form a circular “ring” data path. When data is transferred in a ring topology, the data is sent in one direction along the single continuous pathway. Each device has a repeater which will forward the data until it reaches the device in the topology that the data was intended for.
■ How ring topologies enhance network redundancy
The redundant ring topology provides a convenient way to enhance the redundancy of your network by eliminating a single point of failure. In the case that a device in the ring fails, the backup ring will link every other device to each other. Therefore, data can continue being transported to other nodes in a ring even if a network node goes down.
In addition to preventing communication failure, this topology also allows for easy maintenance. the ring topology isolates the individual cable failures to one network segment for easier repair.
■ HRUI ring redundancy solutions
As mentioned above, we recognize the importance of a reliable, redundant network. All HRUI Industrial managed switches support the ring network redundancy function. Using the market’s open standard ITU-T under G.8032 ERPS (Ethernet ring protection switch) protocol, HRUI devices have a minimal network recovery time of less than 12ms. The ERPS protocol also provides recovery switching for Ethernet traffic while preventing loops from forming at the Ethernet layer.

BT PoE High-power Power Supply Technology
The PoE standard has evolved. Currently there are three main standards: IEEE 802.3 af, IEEE 802.3 at and IEEE 802.3 bt. The 802.3bt standard is backward compatible with 802.3at and 802.3af, and the power can be expanded to 90W. As it breaks through the power limitation, BT PoE greatly expands the application scenarios of PoE technology and supports more terminal devices.

If the cameras don’t output traffic, the cameras will be judged to be down, and the PoE switches will restart the front-end cameras automatically. Manual operation is not required anymore, and timely and reliable solutions can be provided for the later operation and maintenance of the project.

Nowadays, the economy and society develops fastly and rapidly, the network devices are being widely used and becoming more and more power-hungry. So the PoE technology wins a good reputation among users with the capability to provide higher power and reduce the number of cables required.
What Is PoE?
Power over Ethernet (PoE) is a technology that allows network switches to transmit both power and data through an Ethernet cable simultaneously.
What Is A PoE Switch?
PoE switch power over Ethernet switch is a network switch, which applies Power over Ethernet technology. With a PoE network switch, the network connectivity and the power to run the PD (powered device) can both be efficiently realized over the Ethernet cable.
Why Do You Need the PoE Switch?
The traditional switches can not supply power for end devices over Ethernet. This requires additional PSEs and extension cables. However, PoE switches minimizing cable usage and makes things easier by saving costs on power outlets, infrastructure equipment and electrical installation.Based on the working mode of PoE vs. non-PoE switch, we can know that the PoE switch brings benefits over the following aspects:
1) Simple And Convenient
Simplify the installation and streamline the deployment—no need for electricians.
2) Cost-Efficiency
No need for additional cables and power adapters—reduce costs on infrastructure.
3) Flexibility
More placement options allow for deployment in complex environments.
4) Power Management
Intelligently protects your devices from power surges and saves power usages.

PoE System Composition And Working Process
2024-12-26
A complete PoE system includes two parts: Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE) and Powered Device (PD). PSE equipment is a device that supplies power to Ethernet client devices, and it is also the manager of the entire PoE ethernet power supply process. The PD device is a PSE load that accepts power, that is, the client device of the PoE system, such as IP phones, IP cameras, APs, and many other ethernet devices such as PDAs or mobile phone chargers.
What Can You Power with PoE Switch?
PoE switches are separated by their supported standards. Before choosing your PoE solutions, you need to be aware of how much power your devices draw. With that information, you’ll know which standard and business solution suits your needs.
PoE System Working Process
1)PD detection
The PSE outputs a low voltage before supplying power to the powered device to detect whether the powered device (PD) complies with the IEEE802.3af/at/bt standard.
2)Power classification
When the PD of the receiving end device is detected, the PoE device will classify the PD device and evaluate the power loss required by the PD device.
3)Start power supply
After confirming the classification, PSE will output 48V DC to the powered device and confirm that the powered device does not exceed the power requirement of 15.4W.
4)Real-time Monitoring
Provides a stable and reliable 48V DC power for PD equipment to meet the power consumption of PD equipment that does not exceed 15.4W/30W/60-90W.
5)Disconnect power
If the PD device is disconnected from the network, the PSE will quickly (usually within 300-400ms) stop powering the PD device and repeat the detection process to detect whether the cable terminal is connected to the PD device.

Understanding PoE Switches: The Key to Efficient Power and Data Transmission in Modern Network Devices
2025-02-18
In today’s technology-driven world, modern network devices increasingly rely on long cables for power transmission. As these devices require more power, cable usage is also on the rise, leading to unnecessary complexity in setups. This is where Power over Ethernet (PoE) technology significantly changes the game. PoE allows for higher power transmission while minimizing cable clutter compared to traditional methods. One crucial component in the PoE landscape is the PoE switch. In this article, we'll explore what PoE switches are, how they function, and why they are essential for modern network applications.
A Primer on PoE Technology
Power over Ethernet (PoE) is an innovative networking feature that enables network cables to deliver both electrical power and data simultaneously to devices. While data and power travel along the same cable, they utilize different sets of wires, ensuring effective communication between various types of connected devices. This interoperability is key to the seamless functioning of any networking environment.
What are PoE Devices?
PoE technology is composed of two main components: Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE) and Powered Devices (PD). PSE refers to the equipment that transmits power, which includes PoE switches. The devices that receive power, such as IP cameras and VoIP phones, are classified as PDs.
How Do PoE Switches Work?
PoE switches are designed with a straightforward configuration, featuring multiple Ethernet ports to provide a stable power supply and facilitate network communication. Depending on the application, PoE switches operate in two primary configurations:
Mode A Configuration:
In this mode, power and data are transmitted over the same wire.
Mode B Configuration:
Here, separate wires are used for power and data transmission.
Three Key Benefits of PoE Switches
PoE switches have surged in popularity due to their numerous advantages:
Reliability:
Unlike traditional power distribution methods, PoE switches consolidate power management into a single source. They are compatible with various devices, can be easily reset or disabled, and can be equipped with battery backups for uninterrupted service.
Flexibility:
By transmitting power and data through standard Ethernet cables, PoE switches eliminate the need for extra cables. Devices connected to these switches can be relocated with ease, contributing to a cleaner installation and enhancing operational efficiency.
Cost-efficiency:
PoE switches significantly reduce the need for additional electrical cabling, resulting in lower installation and maintenance costs. The straightforward installation process often requires no specialized training, allowing for substantial savings in both time and labor.
Key Applications of PoE Switches
Due to their benefits, PoE switches are increasingly deployed across various applications, including:
IP Cameras:
Many networked surveillance cameras leverage PoE technology to receive both power and data from PoE switches. This has become crucial for enhancing security in commercial and industrial settings. VERSITRON’s PoE switches, for instance, allow for extended IP camera signaling over fiber optic cables, bolstering security and extending installation distances.
Wireless Networks:
PoE switches have played a fundamental role in the expansion of wireless networks, significantly lowering the costs associated with installing access points and controllers. Devices like Bluetooth applications, RFID readers, and Wi-Fi access points benefit greatly from PoE technology, allowing for flexible installation and movement.
VoIP Phones:
Utilizing a single connection, PoE technology has facilitated the growing adoption of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) phones in business environments, streamlining communication.
Conclusion
Understanding the functionality and advantages of PoE switches is vital for leveraging their capabilities in various applications. As the demand for reliable and versatile network solutions grows, sourcing PoE devices from reputable manufacturers becomes increasingly important. HRUI stands out as a leading provider of commercial and industrial PoE switches in various configurations, supporting Ethernet, Fast Ethernet, and Gigabit Ethernet applications over fiber. Investing in quality PoE switches ensures enhanced, secure communication links for a wide range of networking needs.

Do You Really Need CAT6A Cables? Four Key Considerations!
2025-02-26
In the increasingly interconnected world we live in, reliable and high-speed internet connectivity is a necessity for both professional and personal use. With various Ethernet cable options available, CAT6A cables have gained significant popularity.
The difference between CAT6 cables and CAT6A cables.
CAT5 cables are seldom used nowadays; for gigabit network transmission, at least they are necessary. Those with a bigger budget might option for CAT6 or CAT6A cables. Is it really essential to use those cables?
Let's first take a look at the parameters.
CAT6 cable
has a transmission frequency of 250MHz, making it most suitable for applications with transmission rates exceeding 1Gbps, primarily used for Gigabit Ethernet (1000Mbps). The appearance and structure of CAT6 twisted pair cable differ from that of CAT5 or CAT5E twisted pair cables, as it not only features an enhanced insulated cross structure that places the four pairs of wires into the four grooves of the cross, but the diameter of the cable is also thicker.
CAT6A:
The transmission frequency is 500 MHz, and the maximum transmission speed can reach 10 Gbps. CAT6A cables are an improved version of CAT6 cables and can be divided into two types: F/UTP cables and U/UTP cables.
U/UTP twisted pair: This refers to what is commonly known as UTP twisted pair, which is unshielded twisted pair.
F/UTP twisted pair: This type has a total shielding layer made of aluminum foil, and it is a twisted pair without shielding for the individual pairs.
Conclusion
Speed
Price
Material
CAT6A cables have a higher transmission frequency and bandwidth (500 MHz) compared to CAT6 cables (250 MHz), enabling speeds of 10 Gbps versus 1 Gbps for CAT6.
CAT6A cables are significantly more expensive than CAT6 cables, with a 100-meter CAT6 costing about 40% less.
The conductor materials vary: non-shielded CAT6 cables use 0.545±0.02mm conductors, while other types and CAT6A cables use 0.57±0.02mm conductors.
The application of CAT6A cables.
However, before investing in these cables, it's essential to evaluate whether they are necessary for your specific needs. Here are four key considerations to help you make an informed decision.
Bandwidth and Speed Requirements
One primary consideration when choosing cabling is your bandwidth and speed requirements. CAT6A cables support up to 10 Gigabits per second (Gbps) data rates over a maximum distance of 100 meters, providing a robust option for data-intensive applications. If your network demands high-speed internet access for streaming, gaming, large file transfers, or supporting multiple devices concurrently, CAT6A is advantageous.
In contrast, if your usage is limited to basic tasks like web browsing, email, and light streaming, then lower-grade cables such as CAT5E or CAT6 may suffice. Assessing your current and future bandwidth needs is essential to determine if investing in CAT6A is necessary for optimal performance.
Cost vs. Benefit
Finally, the cost versus benefit of CAT6A cables is a vital point of consideration. While they provide superior performance and durability compared to CAT5E and CAT6, CAT6A cables typically come at a higher price point. Organizations and individuals must weigh the upfront investment against the anticipated benefits, including improved performance, increased bandwidth, and future-proofing capabilities.
It’s essential to conduct a cost-benefit analysis to determine if the additional expense aligns with your needs. Small businesses or households with limited networking requirements might find the cost of CAT6A unjustifiable, while larger enterprises or tech-savvy users may see the value in a more capable and robust solution.
Future-Proofing Your Network
As internet speeds and technology continue to advance, investing in future-proofing your network becomes imperative. CAT6A cables are designed to handle emerging technologies and higher data rates, making them a solid choice for long-term investment.
If you foresee expanding your network or implementing high-bandwidth applications such as virtual reality, cloud computing, or data centers, CAT6A is capable of accommodating these advancements seamlessly. Investing in CAT6A cables is a proactive step towards ensuring that your network remains competitive and reliable in the face of rapid technological evolution.
Installation Environment
Consider the installation environment when choosing cabling. CAT6A cables are thicker and less flexible than their predecessors due to their design, which includes additional shielding to reduce interference and crosstalk. While this added shielding is beneficial for performance in high-interference environments, it can pose challenges in cramped spaces or when bending is involved.
If you're installing cables in tight places, such as walls or tight bends, opt for low-profile solutions or consider the implications of CAT6A's size and rigidity. Understanding your installation environment can significantly influence your decision on whether to invest in CAT6A or an alternative with greater adaptability.
Conclusion
Deciding whether you need CAT6A cables depends on a variety of factors including your speed requirements, plans for future growth, potential interference in your environment, and your existing infrastructure. As high-speed internet becomes more vital in both business and domestic settings, it may be wise to invest in CAT6A cables to future-proof your network.
Additionally, pairing them with a powerful switch like the HRUI 2.5G/10G Ethernet Switch can propel your network capabilities to new heights, ensuring you're well-prepared for whatever the digital future holds.

What Is a PoE Injector? A Complete Guide to How It Works and When to Use One
2026-07-13
Learn how a PoE injector works, when it is the right choice, and how it compares with a PoE switch for modern network deployments.
Power over Ethernet (PoE) has become a standard technology for powering IP cameras, wireless access points, VoIP phones, and other network devices through a single Ethernet cable. While PoE switches are widely used, not every network requires replacing an existing switch.
In many cases,
a PoE injector
provides a simple and cost-effective way to add PoE capability without changing the existing network infrastructure.
This guide explains what a PoE injector is, how it works, and when it is the right solution for your network.
What Is a PoE Injector?
A PoE injector
, also known as a
Power over Ethernet injector
, is a device that combines electrical power and Ethernet data into a single network cable. It enables a standard,
non-PoE switch or router to power PoE-compatible devices without replacing existing networking equipment.
Typical powered devices include:
IP Cameras
Wireless Access Points (AP)
VoIP Phones
IoT Devices
Video Intercom Systems
How Does a PoE Injector Work?
A PoE injector sits between the network switch and the powered device.
The process is straightforward:
1. A non-PoE switch sends Ethernet data to the injector.
2. The injector adds electrical power to the Ethernet cable.
3. The cable carries both power and data to the powered device.
For IEEE 802.3af/at/bt compliant injectors, the injector first performs a detection and power-classification process to confirm that the connected device supports PoE before supplying power. This protects non-PoE devices from accidental damage.
PoE Injector vs. PoE Switch
Although both devices deliver power over E
thernet, they are designed for different deployment needs.

If only a few PoE devices need to be added to an existing network, a PoE injector is often the more economical solution. For larger deployments with many powered devices, a PoE switch offers centralized power management and easier expansion.
When Should You Use a PoE Injector?
A PoE injector is an ideal choice in several common scenarios:
Upgrade an Existing Network
If your current Ethernet switch does not support PoE, an injector allows you to power compatible devices without replacing the switch.
Small Deployments
For installations with one or two IP cameras or wireless access points, a PoE injector provides a simple and practical solution.
Reduce Upgrade Costs
Replacing an entire switch solely to support a few PoE devices may not be cost-effective. An injector can significantly reduce deployment costs while delivering the required functionality.

IEEE 802.3af/at/bt compliant

Recommended for most enterprise and commercial networks
Passive PoE Injectors

PoE Standard

Network Speed
– Ensure support for Fast Ethernet, Gigabit, 2.5G, 5G, or 10G if required.
Power Output

Future Expansion
– Higher-power, multi-gig injectors can better support future network upgrades.

It enables both power and data to be delivered over a single Ethernet cable, eliminating the need for additional power outlets while supporting devices such as IP cameras, wireless access points, VoIP phones, and other IEEE 802.3af/at/bt compliant powered devices.

Whether you're building a home network, deploying IP surveillance, or upgrading an office LAN, you'll eventually face one question:
Should I use a hub, a switch, or a router?
Although these devices all connect network equipment, they serve
completely different purposes. Choosing the wrong one can limit performance, reduce security, and create unnecessary network bottlenecks.
In this g
uide, we'll explain the differences in plain English—with practical examples instead of technical jargon.

What Is a Hub?
hub
is the most basic networking device.
Think of it as a loudspeaker in a room. Whenever one device sends data, the hub repeats that information to
every connected device
, whether they need it or not.
Instead of broadcasting traffic everywhere, it learns the
MAC address
of each connected device and remembers which port each device uses.
How it works
If Computer A wants to send data to Computer B, the hub doesn't know which port Computer B is connected to.
Instead, it simply forwards the data to
all ports
Every connected device receives the packet and checks whether it is the intended recipient.
Advantages
Low cost
Simple to install
No configuration required
Limitations
Heavy network congestion
Shared bandwidth
Lower security
Poor scalability
Because every device shares the same communication channel, only one transmission can occur at a time.
Today, hubs have almost disappeared from modern networks.
What Is a Switch?
network switch
is much smarter than a hub.
When data arrives, the switch sends it
only to the correct destination
Example
Imagine four PCs connected to a switch.
If PC1 sends data to PC3:
PC3 receives the packet.
PC2 and PC4 never see the traffic.
Other devices can continue communicating simultaneously.
This greatly improves network efficiency.
Benefits
Higher throughput
Less network congestion
Better security
Full-duplex communication
Dedicated bandwidth per port
Suitable for large networks
Modern switches also support features such as:
VLAN
QoS
Link Aggregation
PoE
Loop Prevention
Network Management
These capabilities make switches the foundation of today's Ethernet networks.
What Is a Router?
router
connects
different networks
Its most common job is connecting your local network to the Internet.
Unlike switches, routers work with
IP addresses
instead of MAC addresses.
Their job is to determine:
Where data should go
Which path is the fastest
Which route is currently available
That's why routers are responsible for moving traffic between different networks.
Many routers also provide:
NAT
DHCP
Firewall protection
VPN
Wi-Fi
Internet sharing
An Easy Way to Remember
Imagine you're trying to deliver a birthday invitation to your friend Emma.

You stand in the lobby and yell：
"Emma! I have your invitation!"
Every
one hears you.
Most people ignore the message.
Only Emma responds.
It works—but it's noisy and inefficient.
The Switch: Looking at the Office Directory
You check the office directory.
It tells you exactly where Emma sits.
You walk directly to her desk and hand over the invitation.
No one else is interrupted.
Fast and efficient.
The Router: Traveling to Another City
Now
Emma works in another city.
You first decide:
Which hig
hway to take
Which exit to use
Which streets to follow
The router works the same way—it chooses the best route between different networks.

PoE Switch for IP Cameras: How to Choose the Right CCTV Network Switch?
2026-07-29
A PoE switch is the preferred network switch for most IP camera systems. It delivers power and data through one Ethernet cable, simplifying installation and reducing cabling costs.
To choose the right PoE switch for CCTV, focus on five factors: PoE budget, port count, uplink speed, management features, and installation environment.
Calculate the PoE Budget
Check the maximum power consumption of every camera before selecting a switch.
Fixed cameras usually use standard PoE or PoE+. PTZ cameras, infrared cameras, and cameras with heaters may require higher power. Use the camera’s maximum rated power—not only its normal operating power—to calculate the total requirement.
Required PoE budget = total camera power + power reserve
A power reserve helps maintain stable operation when IR lighting, PTZ movement, or additional cameras increase the load.
Select Enough PoE Ports
Choose a switch with enough ports for the current system and future expansion.
Up to 8 cameras: 8-port PoE switch
8–16 cameras: 16-port PoE switch
16–24 cameras: 24-port PoE switch
Larger projects: multiple PoE switches with fiber uplinks
Selecting spare ports now can reduce upgrade costs later.
Choose the Right Uplink Speed
A Gigabit PoE switch is a practical choice for most modern CCTV systems. It supports high-resolution cameras and provides sufficient bandwidth for small and medium projects.
For larger systems, multiple 4K cameras, or several access switches, choose a switch with Gigabit SFP fiber uplinks or higher-speed uplinks. This helps prevent bottlenecks between the camera network, NVR, and core network.
Fiber uplinks are also suitable for long-distance connections between buildings or outdoor surveillance locations.
Managed or Unmanaged PoE Switch?
An unmanaged PoE switch is suitable for simple, small-scale CCTV systems. It is easy to deploy and requires no configuration.
A managed PoE switch is recommended for enterprise surveillance, campuses, smart buildings, and multi-switch networks. Key functions may include:
VLAN isolation for separating camera traffic
PoE monitoring and remote camera restart
Traffic management for improved network control
Remote management and fault diagnosis
For professional surveillance systems, managed PoE switching improves visibility and simplifies maintenance.
Match the Switch to the Environment
Commercial PoE switches are suitable for offices, shops, hotels, and indoor camera installations.
For factories, transportation systems, outdoor cabinets, and other demanding locations, use an industrial PoE switch. Industrial models are designed for harsh environments and typically provide wider operating temperatures, stronger surge protection, and more robust hardware.
Plan for Long-Distance Cameras
Standard Ethernet cable runs are typically limited to 100 meters. For remote cameras in parking areas, warehouses, campuses, or industrial sites, consider:
PoE Extend Mode
PoE extenders
Fiber uplinks
Industrial PoE switches near the camera location
These options help maintain stable power and network connectivity over longer distances.
HRUI PoE Switches for CCTV Systems
HRUI provides PoE switches for IP camera and surveillance applications, including desktop, rack-mounted, managed, and industrial models.
Depending on the model, HRUI PoE switches offer Gigabit ports, SFP uplinks, PoE priority, VLAN isolation, Extend Mode, and PoE Watchdog. These functions help installers build reliable and scalable CCTV networks for indoor, outdoor, and industrial applications.
Conclusion
The right PoE switch for IP cameras provides enough power, sufficient ports, reliable uplinks, and features suited to the installation environment.
Before purchasing, confirm the PoE budget, camera quantity, uplink requirement, management needs, and transmission distance. This will help ensure stable video transmission and easier long-term maintenance.

So, what is Access Point Mode, how does it differ from Router Mode, and when should you use it?
This guide explains the basics and provides a practical reference for network installers, system integrators, distributors, and IT professionals.
What
Is an Access Point
A Wireless Access Point, commonly called an AP, is a network device that provides Wi-Fi access to wireless clients and connects them to an existing wired network.
A typical deployment looks like:
Internet → Router/Firewall → Switch → Access Point → Wi-Fi Devices
The router or firewall handles network gateway functions such as routing, NAT, and DHCP, while the AP focuses on providing wireless connectivity.
Dedicated APs are commonly deployed in offices, commercial buildings, schools, hotels, and other environments where multiple areas require reliable Wi-Fi coverage.
Modern APs are available in different Wi-Fi generations, including Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7, providing options for different network requirements and deployment scenarios.
What Is Access Point Mode?
Ac
ess Point Mode is an
opcer
ating mode that allows a compatible router or wireless device to work as an access point instead of acting as a separate router.
When AP Mode is enabled, functions such as routing, NAT, and DHCP are generally disabled or handled by the upstream router. The device connects to the existing LAN and provides Wi-Fi access to connected clients.
In simple terms:
Router Mode:
The device manages the network.
Access Point Mode:
The device extends the existing network through Wi-Fi.
This makes AP Mode useful when an existing router or gateway is already in place but additional wireless coverage is required.

Internet → Main Router → PoE Switch → AP → Wireless Clients
For example, an office may already have a router and Ethernet network but experience weak Wi-Fi coverage in meeting rooms or other areas.
Instead of adding another router and creating another network, an AP can be connected to the existing LAN to provide additional Wi-Fi coverage.

The exact steps vary by manufacturer, but the general process is straightforward.

e device's management interface and select
Access Point Mode

For multiple APs, consistent wireless settings can make network management easier
4. Check the Network Connection
After configuration, connect a wireless device to the AP and verify that it receives an IP address from the main router and can access the network normally.
When Should You Use Access Point Mode?
Expanding Wi-Fi Cov
erage
AP Mode is useful when an existing network needs additional Wi-Fi coverage without replacing the main router.

Multi-floor buildings

oiding Mu
ltiple Routing Layers

Router/Firewall → Network Switch → Multiple APs

oors, or areas.

Access Point
normally uses a wired network connection as its backhaul:
Wired Network → AP → Wi-Fi Clients
Wireless Repeater
receives an existing Wi-Fi signal and retransmits it to extend wireless coverage.
For professional network deployments, a wired AP connection is generally preferred when Ethernet cabling is available because it provides a dedicated wired backhaul.

Why Does a PoE Switch Keep Rebooting?
A PoE switch that repeatedly reboots can interrupt IP cameras, wireless access points, VoIP phones, and other connected devices.
Before replacing the equipment, first determine w
hether the switch itself is rebooting or only the connected PoE devices are restarting. This helps narrow down the possible causes.

Com

1. Unstable Power Supply
An unstable AC/DC input, loose connection, or faulty power adapter can cause the entire switch to restart.
Check the power cable, adapter, UPS, and power source. If possible, test with a known-good power supply.
2. Insufficient PoE Power Budget
A PoE switch has a total power budget for all connected devices.
For example, 10 devices requiring up to 20 W each may require:
10 × 20 W = 200 W
If the available PoE budget is insufficient, connected devices may fail to start or repeatedly lose power.
When designing a PoE network, calculate the maximum expected load and leave reasonable power headroom.
3. Overcurrent or Faulty PoE Device
A faulty IP camera, AP, or other powered device may draw excessive current. Some devices may also require more power during startup.
Disconnect the PoE devices and reconnect them one at a time. If the problem appears after connecting a specific device, test it on another known-good PoE port.
4. Faulty Ethernet Cable
Damaged cables, poor RJ45 terminations, loose connectors, or excessive cable length can cause unstable PoE delivery.
Try a short, known-good Ethernet cable. If the device becomes stable, inspect the original cable path.
For standard Ethernet deployments, the total copper link between the switch and device should generally remain within 100 m.
5. Overheating
High ambient temperature and insufficient ventilation can affect switch stability.
Check the cabinet ventilation, airflow, dust accumulation, and installation environment. For outdoor or harsh industrial applications, use equipment designed for the required operating temperature range.
6. Network Loops or Abnormal Traffic
A reboot-like symptom is not always caused by PoE.
Network loops, broadcast storms, or abnormal traffic can cause temporary connectivity loss, making a PoE device appear to have restarted.
Check the network topology, traffic conditions, and loop-protection settings.

If the problem persists, review logs and seek technical support.
What Is PoE Watchdog?
PoE Watchdog addresses a different problem:
the switch is working normally, but a connected PoE device becomes unresponsive.
On supported PoE switches, it can detect an unresponsive device and automatically restart power on the affected port. This is useful for remote IP cameras, wireless APs, and other unattended deployments.

Entire switch loses power → Check power, thermal, and hardware conditions
Application Example: IP Camera Network
If several IP cameras repeatedly restart, check the
PoE budget, cables, individual cameras, PoE ports, temperature, and switch power
in sequence.
This helps determine whether the problem originates from the switch, camera, cable, or power system without unnecessarily replacing equipment.
For larger CCTV deployments, select a PoE switch with sufficient power capacity and appropriate port specifications for the connected devices.
FAQ
Q: Why does my PoE switch keep rebooting?
A: Common causes include unstable power, insufficient PoE capacity, overcurrent, faulty cables or devices, overheating, and network problems. First determine whether the entire switch or only the PoE devices are restarting.
Q: Can an insufficient PoE budget cause a switch to reboot?
A: An insufficient PoE budget usually causes connected devices to lose power or fail to start. If the entire switch is rebooting, also check its main power supply and thermal conditions.
Q: Why does my IP camera keep restarting?
A: Check the camera's power requirement, available PoE budget, Ethernet cable, PoE port, and possible overcurrent conditions.
Q: Can a bad Ethernet cable cause PoE problems?
A: Yes. Damaged cables, poor connections, and excessive cable length can cause unstable power delivery and intermittent connectivity.
Q: What is PoE Watchdog?
A: PoE Watchdog monitors connected PoE devices and can automatically restart a port when a powered device becomes unresponsive. It is useful for remote cameras, APs, and other unattended devices.
Conclusion
A rebooting PoE switch is not necessarily a hardware failure. Check the
power supply, PoE budget, connected devices, cabling, temperature, and network conditions
systematically before replacing equipment.

Wi-Fi 7 Is Changing Enterprise Ethernet: Why Multi-Gigabit Switching Matters
2026-09-22
Wi-Fi 7 is moving into mainstream enterprise deployment, bringing higher wireless throughput and greater demands on the wired network behind each access point. As a result, upgrading the AP alone may not deliver the expected performance if the Ethernet infrastructure remains limited to Gigabit connections.
Does Wi-Fi 7 Require 2.5G Ethernet?
Not every Wi-Fi 7 deployment requires 2.5G Ethernet, but
2.5G is becoming a practical access speed for enterprise Wi-Fi 7 networks.
It provides more bandwidth than Gigabit Ethernet while supporting many existing copper cabling environments.
The 2026 Ethernet Alliance Roadmap identifies 2.5G, 5G and 10GBASE-T as important enterprise technologies for Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 networks.
For this reason, a typical high-performance deployment can be structured as:
Wi-Fi 7 AP → 2.5G Ethernet → Multi-Gigabit PoE Switch → 10G Uplink
Why Does Wi-Fi 7 Need 10G Uplinks?
The requirement comes from traffic aggregation. A switch connecting multiple 2.5G Wi-Fi 7 APs can quickly carry several gigabits of traffic toward the aggregation or core layer.
10G uplink
provides additional capacity and helps reduce oversubscription, particularly in high-density wireless environments. This makes uplink bandwidth an important consideration when selecting a switch for Wi-Fi 7.
What Type of Switch Is Needed for Wi-Fi 7?
There is no single switch specification for every deployment. The right switch should match the AP's bandwidth, power requirements and network density.
Key considerations include:
2.5G or higher Ethernet ports
PoE capacity
suitable for the selected APs
10G uplinks
for aggregated traffic
Compatible cabling
for the target Ethernet speed
Sufficient
switching capacity
for the deployment
Gigabit Ethernet can still support Wi-Fi 7 in lower-throughput scenarios, but it may limit the usable capacity of higher-performance APs.
As Wi-Fi 7 adoption expands, multi-gigabit switching is becoming an important part of enterprise wireless infrastructure.
The upgrade should therefore be considered end to end, from the AP and PoE access layer to the uplink and aggregation network.

Industrial Ethernet for AI-Powered Machine Vision: What the Network Needs to Handle
2026-09-23
AI-powered machine vision is moving beyond simple inspection tasks. In modern factories, cameras and sensors are increasingly used for defect detection, process monitoring, worker safety, and automated decision-making. As these applications become more data-intensive, the industrial network connecting cameras, edge systems, and control equipment becomes part of the performance equation.
So, what does an industrial Ethernet network need to handle AI-powered machine vision?
Higher Bandwidth at the Edge
Machine vision systems can generate continuous streams of high-resolution image and video data. When multiple cameras operate simultaneously, a traditional 1G connection may become a constraint, particularly when image data is processed or transferred at the edge.
The required Ethernet speed depends on camera resolution, frame rate, compression, and the number of connected devices. For higher-throughput applications,
2.5G, 5G, or 10G
Ethernet can provide additional capacity between cameras, edge computing systems, and aggregation switches.
This makes the access switch an important part of the machine vision architecture:
Industrial Cameras → PoE Switch → Edge Computing → Industrial Network
Does AI Machine Vision Require PoE?
Not necessarily, but PoE can simplify camera deployment by carrying both power and data over a single Ethernet cable. This is particularly useful when cameras are distributed across production lines, warehouses, or other industrial environments.
The switch should be selected according to the camera's power requirements, total PoE budget, port speed, and environmental conditions. For higher-power devices, PoE+ or higher-power PoE technologies may be required.
Why Do Latency and Reliability Matter?
Machine vision is often connected to real-time production processes. Delays or intermittent connectivity can affect how quickly image data reaches an edge system or control application.
For this reason, industrial Ethernet design should consider more than bandwidth.
Low and predictable latency, network redundancy, and rapid fault recovery
can be important in applications where continuous data transmission is required.
Managed industrial switches can support functions such as VLAN, QoS, ring redundancy, and traffic monitoring to help organize and protect machine vision traffic.
Designing the Network for Industrial AI
There is no single Ethernet specification for every AI-powered factory. Network requirements depend on the cameras, computing architecture, production process, and environmental conditions.
A practical design should evaluate:
Port speed:
1G, 2.5G, 5G, or 10G based on traffic requirements
PoE budget:
sufficient power for connected cameras and devices
Uplinks
adequate capacity between access and aggregation layers
Redundancy:
ring or dual-path architectures where required
Industrial protection:
temperature range, surge protection, and power redundancy
As AI moves closer to the factory floor, machine vision is becoming a networking challenge as well as a computing challenge. A well-designed industrial Ethernet infrastructure provides the bandwidth, power, and reliability needed to connect cameras with the systems that turn visual data into production decisions.

Compact. Reliable. Budget-Friendly.
HR-AFR-31+ is a Fast Ethernet PoE extender designed for cost-effective network and IP surveillance deployment. Featuring 1× Fast Ethernet PoE IN port and 3× Fast Ethernet PoE OUT ports, it extends both power and data over a single Ethernet cable — reducing cabling costs while simplifying installation. Supporting IEEE 802.3af/at PoE standards, it delivers stable power and 10/100M connectivity for IP cameras, access points, and other PoE-powered devices.
Compliant with IEEE 802.3, 802.3u, and 802.3x standards, the extender supports 10/100Mbps auto-negotiation, Auto MDI/MDIX, and a long-range mode (activated via DIP switch) that extends PoE and data transmission up to 250 meters at 10Mbps. Real-time LED status indicators enable quick fault analysis. With flexible desktop, wall-mount, or DIN-rail installation, the HR-AFR-31+ is ideal for small-to-medium projects such as offices, retail stores, parking lots, and budget-conscious surveillance deployments.

• Ethernet Ports support 10/100 self-adaptive.
• The panel indicator LEDs will monitor the working status and assist in fault analysis.
• Support automatic port flipping (Auto MDI/MDIX).
• Support Extend mode.
• Having network and PoE relay extension roles.
• Flow control method, full duplex adopts IEEE 802.3x standard, and half duplex adopts Back pressure standard.

By integrating power delivery into a single cable, these switches streamline cabling infrastructure and eliminate the need for separate power sources, thereby providing an efficient and cost-effective solution for powering network devices.

All Ethernet ports on our switches support MDI/MDIX compatibility, allowing for easy setup with no software installation or configuration needed.

The HRUI AI PoE switches provide a range of models featuring both 100M/Gigabit PoE, RJ45, and SFP uplink ports. These switches meet the IEEE 802.3af/at/Hi-PoE standards for Power over Ethernet, with PoE port 1 capable of delivering a maximum output of 60W and other PoE ports capable of 30W. The devices offer three working modes: Default, VLAN (Port Isolation), and Extend. Additionally, the series supports PoE watchdog functionality in both VLAN and Extend modes, enabling the detection and automatic reboot of unresponsive or dropped PoE-powered devices.
With user-friendly installation and maintenance processes, these switches help establish a secure and high-performance network. HRUI AI PoE switches are ideal for various Ethernet access applications, including small to medium-sized enterprises, internet cafes, hotels, and schools.

• Power Over Ethernet

permitting the powering of high-power devices. By integrating power delivery into a single cable, these switches streamline cabling infrastructure and eliminate the need for separate power sources, thereby providing an efficient and cost-effective solution for powering network devices.
• Advanced Functions with DIP Switch
Default:
All ports support communication with each other, with a transmission distance of up to 100 meters and an adaptive speed of 10/100/1000Mbps. This mode disables PoE watchdog on ports.
Extend:
The downlink PoE & data transmission distance of port 9-16 can reach up to 250 meters, with a speed of 10Mbps. This mode enables PoE watchdog on ports.
• AI PoE Watchdog
Detect and reboot dropped or unresponsive PoE-powered devices.
• Safe PoE Smart Boot-up
Support PoE Smart Boot-up that enables PoE on ports from the first to last in sequence to prevent damage to the power supply by sudden large currents. The function is enabled by default.
• A Clear View of Power Usage
The product feature PoE Max indicators, allowing for easy monitoring of power consumption, enabling optimal power usage and ensuring efficient energy management.
• Plug and Play, Easy to Use
All Ethernet ports on our switches support MDI/MDIX compatibility, allowing for easy setup with no software installation or configuration needed.
• 19 Inch Rack Mout
• High Reliable Design
Support installed in a standard rack environment, easy to integrate with other equipment and manage cabling.
Support 4KV surge and 8KV ESD protection.

HR900-AFG-822NS, a high-performance 12-port Gigabit intelligent PoE switch designed for seamless connectivity in modern networking environments. Equipped with premium, high-speed network ICs and a reliable PoE chip, this switch features 8 Gigabit PoE ports, 2 Gigabit Ethernet ports, and 2 Gigabit SFP ports, enabling fast and efficient data transfer across a range of devices.
The switch incorporates advanced AI functionality to automatically enable "AI mode" in Extend mode, optimizing performance for your connected devices. With its intelligent design, the PoE power supply ports automatically detect and provide power to devices compliant with the IEEE 802.3af and IEEE 802.3at standards, ensuring hassle-free integration. Non-PoE devices can transmit data without automatic power detection.
Product Features:
Port Configuration:
8 Gigabit PoE ports, 2 Gigabit Ethernet ports, and 2 Gigabit SFP ports ensure versatile connectivity options.
Standards Compliance:
Fully supports IEEE 802.3, IEEE 802.3u, and IEEE 802.3x standards for reliable networking.
Adaptive RJ45 Ports:
Ethernet ports are self-adaptive, supporting 10/100/1000M speeds for flexible network performance.
Efficient Flow Control:
Implements IEEE 802.3x standard for full duplex and utilizes back pressure for half duplex, enabling efficient network communication.
Extend Mode Functionality:
Ports 7 and 8 can operate in Extend mode, forcing a 10Mbps speed while automatically activating PoE watchdog mode for enhanced device monitoring.
PoE Priority Management:
The switch features default PoE priority, systematically prioritizing power supply from ports 1 to 8.
Status Monitoring:
Panel indicator LEDs provide real-time monitoring of operational status, aiding in fault diagnosis.
Zero Configuration:
Automatically recognizes and allocates power to compatible devices without manual setup.
Surge Protection:
Built-in protection features include 4KV common mode surge protection and ESD ratings of 8KV (air) and 6KV (contact), ensuring robust durability and reliability.

HR-CPE30B-05P is a 2.4GHz wireless bridge featuring 802.3af/at PoE and DC 12V power input for flexible outdoor deployment. Supporting 802.11n 300Mbps wireless transmission with a range of up to 500m, it provides a stable and cost-effective solution for CCTV backhaul, industrial monitoring, building-to-building connectivity, elevator surveillance, and other outdoor networking applications.
Equipped with a built-in 6dBi directional antenna, the device supports PtP, PtMP, and Router modes to meet different networking needs. Features including One-Click Channel Optimization, Hardware Master/Slave switching, Independent Management SSID, and QoS traffic control help improve deployment efficiency and wireless stability. Combined with an IP65-rated enclosure and plug-and-play design, the HR-CPE30B-05P ensures reliable performance in various outdoor environments.
Product Highlights：
1、1*10/100Mbps port.
2、Supporting IP65 protection level shell design, easily adapting to various harsh outdoor environments.
3、Support Standard PoE remote power supply and DC 12V local power supply.
4、Support 802.11n WiFi 300M wireless transmission.
5、Paired with high gain antennas, the transmission distance can reach 500m in an open and unobstructed environment.
6、Support wall mounted and pole mounted installation methods, with simple construction.
7、Automatically selects channels to ensure stable signal.
8、Compatible with mainstream cameras on the market.
9、No configuration required, easy to use.
